I am 53 years old and have farmed these fields in Quzhou since I was a young man. My family has ten mu of good flat land, and I know every corner of it. This year, like most years, I will grow winter wheat and summer maize. The wheat is already in the ground—I sowed it last October after rotary tilling the soil. I use an improved wheat variety because the seeds from the county supply store grow strong and resist lodging. For the maize that follows the wheat harvest in June, I will buy hybrid seed. I do not till before planting the maize; there is no time after the wheat comes off, and everyone around here knows no-tillage works fine if you clear the straw properly. 

For the wheat, I will put down about 50 kilograms of compound fertilizer per mu as a basal dressing—something like 19-22-7—and then topdress with another 25 kilograms of compound and about 20 kilograms of urea at the green-up and jointing stages. That gives the wheat enough strength. The maize only gets one basal dressing of about 45 kilograms of compound fertilizer per mu, usually a high-nitrogen blend like 28-6-6, because by then I am busy and the maize grows fast. I will irrigate the wheat four times—green-up, jointing, heading, and grain filling—and the maize twice, at seedling and big-trumpet stages, using water from our well. For pests, I spray herbicide once on each crop, insecticide twice, and I add one fungicide spray on the wheat when the weather turns humid. I expect the wheat to give me about 500 kilograms per mu and the maize about 550 kilograms per mu, which is enough to feed my family and sell the surplus.
